articles.title: Emergency numbers Singapore
articles.en: In Singapore, call 995 for ambulance or fire emergencies and 999 for police emergencies. If it is safe, state your location clearly and follow the operator’s instructions.

articles.title: CPR
articles.en: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) uses chest compressions to help circulate blood when a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Call emergency services, request an AED and follow dispatcher instructions. Untrained bystanders can perform hands-only compressions.

articles.title: AED
articles.en: An automated external defibrillator (AED) checks heart rhythm and can deliver a shock when indicated. Turn it on and follow its spoken instructions; it will not advise a shock unless appropriate.

articles.title: Heatstroke
articles.en: Heatstroke is a life-threatening condition involving dangerous overheating and neurological symptoms such as confusion or collapse. Call emergency services and cool the person rapidly while waiting for help.

articles.title: Dehydration
articles.en: Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. Signs include thirst, dark urine and dizziness. Severe dehydration, confusion or inability to drink warrants urgent medical attention.

articles.title: Food poisoning
articles.en: Foodborne illness can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps and fever. Hydration is important; seek medical care for bloody stools, severe dehydration, persistent high fever or severe symptoms.

articles.title: Stroke
articles.en: A stroke occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted or bleeding occurs. Sudden face drooping, arm weakness or speech difficulty are warning signs: call emergency services immediately.

articles.title: Heart attack
articles.en: A heart attack occurs when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked. Symptoms can include chest pressure, breathlessness, sweating or discomfort in the arm or jaw. Seek emergency help immediately.

articles.title: First aid
articles.en: First aid is immediate assistance before professional care arrives. Check scene safety, call emergency services for serious conditions and follow evidence-based guidance rather than attempting unfamiliar procedures.

articles.title: Fire safety
articles.en: If a fire starts, alert others, leave by a safe exit and call emergency services. Avoid lifts during building fires and never re-enter a burning building.

articles.title: Earthquake
articles.en: Earthquakes occur when stored stress in Earth’s crust is released. During shaking, drop, cover and hold on; avoid windows and falling objects.

articles.title: Tsunami
articles.en: A tsunami is a series of powerful ocean waves often caused by underwater earthquakes. After strong coastal shaking or a natural warning, move immediately to higher ground and follow official alerts.

articles.title: Flood
articles.en: Flooding occurs when water covers normally dry land. Never walk or drive through moving floodwater; follow evacuation notices and avoid electrical hazards.

articles.title: Haze
articles.en: Haze is airborne pollution that can contain fine particles harmful to the lungs and heart. Reduce strenuous outdoor activity when air quality is poor and follow local health advisories.

articles.title: Air quality index
articles.en: Air quality indices summarize pollution levels and associated health guidance. Different countries use different indices, so interpret values using the local authority’s scale.

articles.title: PM2.5
articles.en: PM2.5 refers to airborne particles with diameters of 2.5 micrometres or less. These particles can penetrate deep into the lungs; exposure is associated with respiratory and cardiovascular risks.

articles.title: N95 respirator
articles.en: A properly fitted N95 respirator filters at least 95 percent of certain airborne test particles under certification conditions. Fit and seal matter; a loose respirator protects less effectively.

articles.title: Water purification
articles.en: Boiling water can kill many disease-causing microorganisms but does not remove chemical pollutants or dissolved salts. Use a suitable treatment method for the suspected contamination.

articles.title: Internet safety
articles.en: Protect online accounts with unique passwords, multifactor authentication and software updates. Be cautious of urgent requests for money, passwords or verification codes.

articles.title: Phishing
articles.en: Phishing is a scam that tricks people into revealing credentials or transferring money through deceptive messages or websites. Verify requests using independently found official contact details.

articles.title: Scams
articles.en: Scams use deception to obtain money, information or access. Pressure, secrecy, guaranteed returns and unusual payment requests are warning signs; verify before acting.

articles.title: Password manager
articles.en: A password manager stores and generates strong unique passwords. Protect it with a strong master password and enable multifactor authentication where available.

articles.title: Two-factor authentication
articles.en: Two-factor authentication adds another verification step beyond a password, such as an authenticator app or security key. It reduces the risk from stolen passwords.

articles.title: Personal finance
articles.en: Personal finance includes budgeting, saving, managing debt, insurance and investing. An emergency fund and understanding interest costs can help improve financial resilience.

articles.title: Budgeting
articles.en: A budget compares income with spending and savings goals. Track essentials, discretionary spending and irregular costs; review it when circumstances change.

articles.title: Compound interest
articles.en: Compound interest means earning interest on previous interest as well as on the original amount. Over time it can accelerate savings growth and also increase unpaid debt.

articles.title: Inflation
articles.en: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money. Individual prices may move differently from the overall inflation rate.

articles.title: Interest rates
articles.en: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing or reward for lending money, usually expressed annually. Actual costs depend on compounding, fees and loan terms.

articles.title: Stocks
articles.en: A stock represents ownership in a company. Share prices can rise or fall, and shareholders may receive dividends, but returns are not guaranteed.

articles.title: Bonds
articles.en: A bond is a debt instrument through which an investor lends money to an issuer. Bonds have interest-rate, credit and liquidity risks, and their prices can fluctuate.

articles.title: Exchange rates
articles.en: An exchange rate describes the value of one currency relative to another. Rates change with economic conditions, interest rates, expectations and market demand.

articles.title: Diversification
articles.en: Diversification spreads investments across different assets to reduce concentration risk. It does not eliminate market losses or guarantee profits.

articles.title: CPF Singapore
articles.en: Singapore’s Central Provident Fund (CPF) is a mandatory social security savings system for eligible workers, supporting retirement, housing and healthcare under applicable rules.

articles.title: HDB Singapore
articles.en: Singapore’s Housing & Development Board (HDB) plans and develops public housing. Eligibility, grants and resale rules vary by scheme and can change.

articles.title: MRT Singapore
articles.en: Singapore’s Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) is an urban rail network connecting residential, commercial and transport hubs. Check current official route information for disruptions.

articles.title: Hawker centres
articles.en: Singapore hawker centres bring together stalls selling affordable local dishes and represent a major part of the country’s food culture.

articles.title: Malay language
articles.en: Malay is an Austronesian language and one of Singapore’s four official languages. It is also Singapore’s national language.

articles.title: Mandarin Chinese
articles.en: Mandarin is a variety of Chinese and one of Singapore’s four official languages. Standard written Chinese is used widely in education and media.

articles.title: Southeast Asia
articles.en: Southeast Asia is a region spanning mainland and maritime countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines.

articles.title: ASEAN
articles.en: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is a regional organization founded in 1967 to promote cooperation among Southeast Asian member states.

articles.title: Malaysia
articles.en: Malaysia is a Southeast Asian country consisting of Peninsular Malaysia and East Malaysian states on Borneo. Its capital is Kuala Lumpur.

articles.title: Indonesia
articles.en: Indonesia is a large archipelagic country in Southeast Asia, with thousands of islands and substantial linguistic, cultural and ecological diversity.

articles.title: China
articles.en: China is a country in East Asia with a long recorded history, a large population and major influence on global trade, culture and technology.

articles.title: Japan
articles.en: Japan is an island country in East Asia, known for its cultural heritage, advanced industries and exposure to earthquakes and volcanic activity.

articles.title: India
articles.en: India is a South Asian country with a large and diverse population, many languages and a long history of cultural and scientific traditions.

articles.title: World War II
articles.en: World War II was a global conflict fought from 1939 to 1945, involving the Axis and Allied powers. It caused immense destruction and loss of life.

articles.title: Democracy
articles.en: Democracy is a system of government in which political authority ultimately rests with the people, often exercised through elections and accountable institutions.

articles.title: United Nations
articles.en: The United Nations is an international organization founded in 1945 to support peace, international cooperation, human rights and development.

articles.title: Human rights
articles.en: Human rights are basic rights and freedoms considered inherent to all people, including protections for life, dignity, liberty and equal treatment.

articles.title: Gravity
articles.en: Gravity is the interaction that attracts objects with mass or energy. It keeps planets in orbit and causes objects near Earth to fall toward the ground.

articles.title: Atoms
articles.en: Atoms are the basic units of chemical elements, consisting of a nucleus surrounded by electrons. Their arrangements determine much of matter’s chemistry.

articles.title: DNA
articles.en: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) carries genetic information in most living organisms. Its sequence helps direct the production of proteins and inheritance of traits.

articles.title: Evolution
articles.en: Biological evolution is change in inherited characteristics of populations over generations. Mechanisms include natural selection, genetic drift and mutation.

articles.title: Vaccines
articles.en: Vaccines train the immune system to recognize specific pathogens or their components. They can reduce the risk of infection or severe disease, depending on the vaccine.

articles.title: Antibiotics
articles.en: Antibiotics treat certain bacterial infections but do not treat viruses. Misuse contributes to antibiotic resistance; take them only as directed by a qualified clinician.

articles.title: Viruses
articles.en: Viruses are infectious agents that replicate inside living cells. Some cause disease, while others infect organisms without obvious symptoms.

articles.title: Bacteria
articles.en: Bacteria are single-celled microorganisms found across many environments. Many are harmless or beneficial, while some cause infections.

articles.title: Nutrition
articles.en: Nutrition concerns how food supplies energy and nutrients needed for health. A balanced diet typically includes varied foods and appropriate amounts of protein, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals.

articles.title: Sleep
articles.en: Sleep supports memory, immune function and physical recovery. Sleep needs vary, but most adults generally benefit from seven to nine hours per night.

articles.title: Exercise
articles.en: Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular, muscular and mental health. Appropriate exercise combines aerobic movement, strength work and recovery.

articles.title: Solar energy
articles.en: Solar energy is energy from sunlight that can be converted into electricity using photovoltaic cells or captured as heat. Output depends on sunlight and system conditions.

articles.title: Electric vehicles
articles.en: Electric vehicles use electric motors and batteries rather than relying solely on combustion engines. Environmental impacts depend partly on electricity generation and manufacturing.

articles.title: Renewable energy
articles.en: Renewable energy comes from naturally replenished sources such as sunlight, wind, flowing water and geothermal heat. Each has different costs and environmental impacts.

articles.title: Cybersecurity
articles.en: Cybersecurity involves protecting systems, networks and information from unauthorized access, disruption and misuse. Effective protection combines technology and user practices.

articles.title: Cloud computing
articles.en: Cloud computing provides computing resources, storage and software over networks on demand. It can improve scalability but requires attention to security and availability.

articles.title: Machine learning
articles.en: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which models learn patterns from data. Performance depends on data quality, design and evaluation.

articles.title: Large language models
articles.en: Large language models are AI systems trained on extensive text to predict and generate language. They can be useful for writing and analysis but may produce inaccurate information.

articles.title: Earth
articles.en: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only world currently known to support life. Its oceans, atmosphere and geology shape climate and ecosystems.

articles.title: Moon
articles.en: The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite. Its gravity contributes to ocean tides, and its phases reflect changing viewing angles of sunlight.

articles.title: Mars
articles.en: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, a cold rocky world with a thin atmosphere and evidence of ancient liquid water.

articles.title: Milky Way
articles.en: The Milky Way is the galaxy containing our Solar System. It includes billions of stars, gas, dust and a supermassive black hole at its centre.

articles.title: Water cycle
articles.en: The water cycle describes the movement of water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff and storage in oceans, land and ice.

articles.title: Carbon cycle
articles.en: The carbon cycle tracks carbon moving among the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans and rocks. Human fossil-fuel use adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.

articles.title: Biodiversity
articles.en: Biodiversity is the variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. It supports ecological resilience and many services people depend on.

articles.title: Deforestation
articles.en: Deforestation is the conversion of forests to other land uses. It can threaten habitats, release stored carbon and alter local water cycles.

articles.title: Recycling
articles.en: Recycling converts suitable discarded materials into new products. Reducing consumption and reusing products often avoid waste before recycling is needed.

articles.title: Critical thinking
articles.en: Critical thinking involves assessing evidence, checking assumptions, comparing explanations and distinguishing reliable information from unsupported claims.

articles.title: Scientific method
articles.en: Scientific inquiry involves asking questions, developing testable hypotheses, collecting evidence and revising conclusions. Methods vary across scientific disciplines.

articles.title: Media literacy
articles.en: Media literacy is the ability to evaluate messages, sources, incentives and evidence across media. Verify claims through multiple credible sources.

articles.title: Time zones
articles.en: Time zones are regions that use standardized local times. Singapore uses UTC+8 throughout the year and does not observe daylight saving time.

articles.title: Latitude and longitude
articles.en: Latitude measures position north or south of the equator; longitude measures position east or west of the prime meridian. Together they identify locations on Earth.

articles.title: Navigation
articles.en: Navigation is the process of planning and following a route. Maps, landmarks, satellite positioning and local signs help determine direction and location.

articles.title: Food safety
articles.en: Food safety includes handwashing, avoiding cross-contamination, thorough cooking and correct storage temperatures to reduce foodborne illness.

articles.title: Mental wellbeing
articles.en: Mental wellbeing includes emotional, psychological and social functioning. Sleep, connection, activity and professional support can help; urgent distress warrants timely assistance.

articles.title: Digital privacy
articles.en: Digital privacy concerns control over personal information online. Review app permissions, limit unnecessary sharing and understand how services collect and use data.

articles.title: Public transport
articles.en: Public transport includes shared buses, trains and other services. It can reduce per-passenger road space and emissions compared with many private-car trips.

articles.title: Electricity
articles.en: Electricity is the movement or presence of electric charge. It powers devices and infrastructure but can cause serious injury if handled unsafely.

articles.title: How computers work
articles.en: Computers process information using hardware such as processors and memory, directed by software instructions. Data is commonly represented in binary form.

articles.title: How the internet works
articles.en: The internet connects networks using common protocols. Devices exchange packets of data through routers, while services such as the web use additional protocols.

articles.title: How search engines work
articles.en: Search engines discover and index information, then rank results for user queries. Ranking considers relevance and other signals; results are not necessarily accurate.

articles.title: Wikipedia
articles.en: Wikipedia is a collaboratively edited online encyclopedia operated by the Wikimedia Foundation. Its articles vary in quality and should be checked against cited sources when accuracy matters.

articles.title: Bond
articles.en: A bond is a debt security: an investor lends money to an issuer in return for interest payments and repayment of principal at maturity, subject to default risk.

articles.title: Government bond
articles.en: A government bond is debt issued by a national government. Its credit risk, currency exposure, maturity and interest-rate sensitivity depend on the issuing country and terms.

articles.title: Corporate bond
articles.en: A corporate bond is debt issued by a company. Investors assess the issuer’s capacity to pay interest and principal, including leverage, cash flow and seniority.

articles.title: Bond yield
articles.en: Bond yield expresses a bond’s return relative to its price. Yield to maturity estimates the annualized return if held to maturity with promised payments made; actual returns may differ.

articles.title: Coupon rate
articles.en: A bond’s coupon rate determines its stated periodic interest payments as a percentage of face value. Coupon rate is distinct from market yield.

articles.title: Yield to maturity
articles.en: Yield to maturity is the discount rate that equates a bond’s price with its scheduled cash flows, assuming payments occur as promised.

articles.title: Duration
articles.en: Bond duration measures sensitivity to interest-rate changes. Higher-duration bonds generally move more in price for a given change in yields.

articles.title: Convexity
articles.en: Convexity describes how a bond’s price sensitivity to yield changes itself changes as yields move. It helps refine duration-based estimates.

articles.title: Credit spread
articles.en: Credit spread is the yield premium over a reference rate or government bond that compensates for credit, liquidity and other risks.

articles.title: Credit rating
articles.en: A credit rating is an agency’s opinion of an issuer’s or instrument’s creditworthiness, not a guarantee against default.

articles.title: Investment-grade bond
articles.en: Investment-grade bonds carry relatively higher agency credit ratings, typically BBB-/Baa3 or above, but still involve credit and market risk.

articles.title: High-yield bond
articles.en: High-yield or speculative-grade bonds have ratings below investment grade and generally offer higher yields in exchange for greater default risk.

articles.title: Default risk
articles.en: Default risk is the possibility that a borrower fails to meet contractual debt payments. Recovery depends on collateral, seniority and insolvency proceedings.

articles.title: Leverage
articles.en: Leverage means using borrowed funds or financial instruments to magnify exposure. It can increase potential returns but also magnifies losses and liquidity risk.

articles.title: Debt-to-equity ratio
articles.en: Debt-to-equity compares a company’s liabilities or interest-bearing debt with shareholder equity, depending on the definition used. It is one measure of financial leverage.

articles.title: Interest coverage ratio
articles.en: Interest coverage compares earnings, commonly EBIT, with interest expense. Lower coverage can indicate reduced ability to service debt.

articles.title: Asset-backed security
articles.en: An asset-backed security (ABS) is backed by a pool of financial assets such as auto loans, credit-card receivables or other contractual cash flows. Investors face underlying borrower and structural risks.

articles.title: Mortgage-backed security
articles.en: A mortgage-backed security (MBS) channels cash flows from pooled mortgages to investors. Key risks include defaults, prepayments and changes in interest rates.

articles.title: Residential mortgage-backed security
articles.en: Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) are backed by home mortgage loans. Cash flows are influenced by borrower repayments, defaults and refinancing.

articles.title: Commercial mortgage-backed security
articles.en: Commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) are backed by commercial property loans, exposing investors to tenant, property valuation and refinancing risks.

articles.title: Collateralized debt obligation
articles.en: A collateralized debt obligation (CDO) pools debt assets and divides payments into tranches with different priorities and risks. Complex structures contributed to financial-crisis vulnerabilities.

articles.title: Collateralized loan obligation
articles.en: A collateralized loan obligation (CLO) securitizes a pool of corporate loans, commonly leveraged loans, into tranches with different risk and return profiles.

articles.title: Securitization
articles.en: Securitization packages financial assets and sells claims on their cash flows to investors, often through a special-purpose vehicle.

articles.title: Tranche
articles.en: A tranche is a layer of a structured security with a defined payment priority. Senior tranches are typically paid before junior tranches, but none are risk-free.

articles.title: Credit enhancement
articles.en: Credit enhancement is a feature intended to reduce investor credit losses, such as subordination, reserve accounts or third-party guarantees.

articles.title: Prepayment risk
articles.en: Prepayment risk arises when borrowers repay loans earlier than expected, changing the timing of cash flows and often reducing reinvestment returns.

articles.title: Interest rate swap
articles.en: An interest rate swap is a derivative in which parties exchange interest payments, often fixed versus floating, on a notional principal.

articles.title: Credit default swap
articles.en: A credit default swap (CDS) transfers specified credit risk: the protection buyer pays premiums and the seller compensates for covered credit events under the contract.

articles.title: Derivative
articles.en: A derivative is a financial contract whose value depends on an underlying asset, rate, index or event. Examples include futures, options and swaps.

articles.title: Option
articles.en: An option gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified price under stated terms.

articles.title: Call option
articles.en: A call option gives its holder the right to buy an underlying asset at a specified strike price before or at expiry, depending on the contract.

articles.title: Put option
articles.en: A put option gives its holder the right to sell an underlying asset at a specified strike price before or at expiry, depending on the contract.

articles.title: Futures contract
articles.en: A futures contract is a standardized agreement traded on an exchange to buy or sell an asset at a specified future date and price, generally with margin requirements.

articles.title: Margin call
articles.en: A margin call is a demand to add funds or collateral when account equity falls below required levels. Positions may be liquidated if requirements are not met.

articles.title: Liquidity risk
articles.en: Liquidity risk is the risk that an asset cannot be sold quickly at a reasonable price or that an entity cannot meet cash obligations when due.

articles.title: Market risk
articles.en: Market risk is potential loss from movements in prices, interest rates, exchange rates or other market variables.

articles.title: Counterparty risk
articles.en: Counterparty risk is the possibility that the other party to a contract fails to meet its obligations.

articles.title: Asset allocation
articles.en: Asset allocation divides investments among asset classes such as equities, bonds and cash based on goals, risk tolerance and time horizon.

articles.title: Exchange-traded fund
articles.en: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is an investment fund whose shares trade on an exchange. It may track an index or follow an active strategy.

articles.title: Unit trust
articles.en: A unit trust is a pooled investment vehicle managed according to a mandate. Investors hold units and bear fund fees and investment risks.

articles.title: Net asset value
articles.en: Net asset value (NAV) is a fund’s assets minus liabilities, usually expressed per share or unit.

articles.title: Dividend
articles.en: A dividend is a distribution of company earnings or capital to shareholders. Dividends are discretionary and may be reduced or suspended.

articles.title: Price-to-earnings ratio
articles.en: The price-to-earnings ratio compares a stock’s price with earnings per share. It can be misleading for loss-making or cyclical companies.

articles.title: Discounted cash flow
articles.en: Discounted cash flow (DCF) estimates an asset’s present value by forecasting future cash flows and discounting them at an appropriate rate.

articles.title: Net present value
articles.en: Net present value (NPV) sums discounted future cash flows minus initial cost. A positive NPV suggests value creation under the chosen assumptions.

articles.title: Internal rate of return
articles.en: Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes a project’s net present value zero. It has limitations with unusual cash-flow patterns.

articles.title: Monetary policy
articles.en: Monetary policy refers to central-bank actions influencing interest rates, money and credit conditions to pursue goals such as price stability.

articles.title: Fiscal policy
articles.en: Fiscal policy uses government taxation and spending to influence economic activity, public services and redistribution.

articles.title: Central bank
articles.en: A central bank manages monetary policy and often oversees financial stability, currency issuance and payment systems.

articles.title: Foreign exchange
articles.en: Foreign exchange (FX) is the conversion of one currency into another. Exchange rates move with economic conditions, policy expectations and capital flows.

articles.title: Currency hedging
articles.en: Currency hedging uses instruments such as forwards or options to reduce exposure to exchange-rate movements, usually at a cost.

articles.title: Structured note
articles.en: A structured note combines a debt instrument with derivative-linked returns. Payouts can be complex and may expose investors to issuer and market losses.

articles.title: Fixed coupon note
articles.en: A fixed coupon note (FCN) typically pays stated coupons linked to the performance of reference assets and may require delivery of an underperforming asset under specified conditions.

articles.title: Knock-in barrier
articles.en: A knock-in barrier is a price threshold that activates a contractual feature if reached, depending on the product’s observation rules.

articles.title: Knock-out barrier
articles.en: A knock-out barrier is a threshold that may terminate or alter a structured product early if specified conditions are met.

articles.title: Real estate investment trust
articles.en: A real estate investment trust (REIT) holds income-producing real estate or related assets and typically distributes substantial income, subject to local rules.

articles.title: Singapore Savings Bonds
articles.en: Singapore Savings Bonds are Singapore Government securities designed for individuals, with step-up interest and monthly redemption opportunities under program rules.

articles.title: Singapore Government Securities
articles.en: Singapore Government Securities (SGS) are debt securities issued by the Singapore government, including Treasury bills and bonds.

articles.title: Treasury bill
articles.en: A Treasury bill is a short-term government debt instrument usually issued at a discount and redeemed at face value at maturity.

articles.title: CPF
articles.en: Singapore’s Central Provident Fund (CPF) is a mandatory social security savings system supporting retirement, housing and healthcare, subject to eligibility and withdrawal rules.

articles.title: Monetary Authority of Singapore
articles.en: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is Singapore’s central bank and integrated financial regulator, responsible for monetary policy and financial-sector oversight.

articles.title: Basel III
articles.en: Basel III is an international banking regulatory framework strengthening capital, liquidity and leverage standards following the global financial crisis.

articles.title: Capital adequacy ratio
articles.en: A capital adequacy ratio compares qualifying regulatory capital with risk-weighted assets, helping assess a bank’s capacity to absorb losses.

articles.title: Non-performing loan
articles.en: A non-performing loan is a loan for which repayment is seriously overdue or otherwise impaired, based on applicable accounting or supervisory definitions.

articles.title: Vietnam War
articles.en: The Vietnam War was a prolonged conflict involving North Vietnam and its allies against South Vietnam and its principal ally, the United States. Major US combat involvement ended in 1973; Saigon fell in 1975, leading to reunification.

articles.title: World War I
articles.en: World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918, drawing major powers into trench warfare and global campaigns. Its aftermath reshaped empires and international politics.

articles.title: Korean War
articles.en: The Korean War began in 1950 when North Korea invaded South Korea. UN-led forces and China intervened; a 1953 armistice ended major fighting without a formal peace treaty.

articles.title: Cold War
articles.en: The Cold War was a geopolitical rivalry, roughly 1947–1991, between the United States and Soviet Union and their allies, marked by nuclear deterrence, proxy wars and ideological competition.

articles.title: Great Depression
articles.en: The Great Depression was a severe worldwide economic downturn beginning in 1929, involving banking failures, mass unemployment and major changes in economic policy.

articles.title: Holocaust
articles.en: The Holocaust was Nazi Germany’s systematic persecution and murder of six million Jews during World War II, alongside persecution and killing of other groups.

articles.title: D-Day
articles.en: D-Day commonly refers to the Allied landings in Normandy on 6 June 1944, opening a major western front against Nazi Germany.

articles.title: Battle of Stalingrad
articles.en: The Battle of Stalingrad (1942–1943) was a pivotal Soviet victory over Nazi German forces on the Eastern Front of World War II.

articles.title: Pearl Harbor attack
articles.en: Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, prompting the United States to enter World War II.

articles.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
articles.en: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, causing mass deaths and contributing to Japan’s surrender amid continuing historical debate.

articles.title: Russian Revolution
articles.en: The Russian Revolutions of 1917 overthrew the tsarist monarchy and later brought the Bolsheviks to power, paving the way for the Soviet Union.

articles.title: Chinese Civil War
articles.en: The Chinese Civil War was fought primarily between Nationalists and Communists; in 1949 the Communist Party established the People’s Republic of China while the Republic of China government retreated to Taiwan.

articles.title: Cultural Revolution
articles.en: China’s Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), launched by Mao Zedong, involved political purges, mass mobilization, violence and major social disruption.

articles.title: Tiananmen Square protests of 1989
articles.en: In 1989, student-led demonstrations in Beijing called for reforms. Chinese authorities used military force to suppress protests in early June; the death toll remains disputed.

articles.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
articles.en: The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November 1989 amid political changes in East Germany, symbolizing the collapse of communist rule in Eastern Europe.

articles.title: September 11 attacks
articles.en: On 11 September 2001, al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked aircraft and attacked the World Trade Center and Pentagon; a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania.

articles.title: Iraq War
articles.en: The US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003 overthrew Saddam Hussein. Claims about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction were not substantiated, and prolonged conflict followed.

articles.title: Afghanistan War
articles.en: Following the September 2001 attacks, US-led forces invaded Afghanistan and toppled the Taliban government. The Taliban returned to power in 2021 after the withdrawal of US forces.

articles.title: Global financial crisis of 2008
articles.en: The 2007–2009 financial crisis involved collapsing US housing-related credit, banking stress and a global recession, prompting major financial rescues and regulatory reforms.

articles.title: COVID-19 pandemic
articles.en: COVID-19 is a disease caused by SARS-CoV-2. The pandemic beginning in 2020 caused widespread illness, deaths and disruption, accelerating vaccine development and public-health responses.

articles.title: Singapore independence
articles.en: Singapore became independent on 9 August 1965 after separating from Malaysia, following a brief period of merger beginning in 1963.

articles.title: Japanese occupation of Singapore
articles.en: Japan occupied Singapore from February 1942 to September 1945. The period brought severe hardship, repression and atrocities including the Sook Ching killings.

articles.title: Fall of Singapore
articles.en: British-led forces surrendered Singapore to Japan on 15 February 1942, a major Allied defeat in the Pacific War.

articles.title: Sook Ching
articles.en: Sook Ching refers to the Japanese military’s screening and mass killing of ethnic Chinese civilians in occupied Singapore and Malaya in 1942.

articles.title: Raffles and Singapore
articles.en: Stamford Raffles established a British trading post in Singapore in 1819, though the island had a much longer precolonial history and existing Malay political ties.

articles.title: Singapore merger with Malaysia
articles.en: Singapore joined the Federation of Malaysia in September 1963 and separated in August 1965 amid political, economic and communal tensions.

articles.title: Singapore racial riots of 1964
articles.en: Communal riots in Singapore in 1964 caused deaths and injuries, highlighting ethnic tensions during the period of merger with Malaysia.

articles.title: Singapore housing development
articles.en: Singapore’s Housing and Development Board, established in 1960, expanded public housing and reshaped the country’s urban and social landscape.

articles.title: Singapore National Service
articles.en: Singapore introduced compulsory National Service in 1967, building a citizen-based defence system after independence.

articles.title: Lee Kuan Yew
articles.en: Lee Kuan Yew was Singapore’s first prime minister from 1959 to 1990 and a central figure in its development, known for state-building and an often-criticized restrictive political approach.

articles.title: Goh Keng Swee
articles.en: Goh Keng Swee was a founding Singapore leader who shaped economic development, defence and education policy after independence.

articles.title: S. Rajaratnam
articles.en: S. Rajaratnam was a founding Singapore minister and foreign-policy architect, associated with multiracial nation-building and the National Pledge.

articles.title: David Marshall
articles.en: David Marshall was Singapore’s first chief minister (1955–1956) and an advocate of self-government, later serving as a diplomat.

articles.title: Lim Yew Hock
articles.en: Lim Yew Hock served as Singapore’s chief minister from 1956 to 1959 during its transition toward full internal self-government.

articles.title: Yusof Ishak
articles.en: Yusof Ishak was Singapore’s first president from 1965 to 1970 and earlier its Yang di-Pertuan Negara; his portrait appears on Singapore banknotes.

articles.title: Lee Hsien Loong
articles.en: Lee Hsien Loong served as Singapore’s third prime minister from 2004 to 2024, overseeing major economic and social policy developments.

articles.title: Lawrence Wong
articles.en: Lawrence Wong became Singapore’s fourth prime minister in May 2024, succeeding Lee Hsien Loong.

articles.title: Mahatma Gandhi
articles.en: Mahatma Gandhi led nonviolent campaigns against British colonial rule in India and became an influential figure in global civil-rights movements.

articles.title: Winston Churchill
articles.en: Winston Churchill was Britain’s prime minister during most of World War II and a prominent wartime leader, whose imperial record remains contested.

articles.title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
articles.en: Franklin D. Roosevelt was US president from 1933 to 1945, leading New Deal reforms and much of the US response to World War II.

articles.title: Adolf Hitler
articles.en: Adolf Hitler was Nazi Germany’s dictator from 1933 to 1945. His regime launched aggressive war in Europe and perpetrated the Holocaust.

articles.title: Joseph Stalin
articles.en: Joseph Stalin led the Soviet Union for decades until 1953, overseeing industrialization, wartime leadership, purges, forced collectivization and mass repression.

articles.title: Mao Zedong
articles.en: Mao Zedong was a principal founder of the People’s Republic of China in 1949. His campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution, caused enormous upheaval and loss of life.

articles.title: Deng Xiaoping
articles.en: Deng Xiaoping was a central Chinese leader behind market-oriented reforms and opening-up policies beginning in the late 1970s.

articles.title: Sun Yat-sen
articles.en: Sun Yat-sen was a Chinese revolutionary and political thinker who helped overthrow the Qing dynasty and is widely regarded as a founding figure of republican China.

articles.title: Chiang Kai-shek
articles.en: Chiang Kai-shek led China’s Nationalist government during much of the war against Japan and the Chinese Civil War, later ruling the Republic of China in Taiwan.

articles.title: Ho Chi Minh
articles.en: Ho Chi Minh was a Vietnamese revolutionary leader and founding president of North Vietnam, central to Vietnamese independence and communist state formation.

articles.title: Vo Nguyen Giap
articles.en: Vo Nguyen Giap was a Vietnamese general prominent in victories over French colonial forces and in North Vietnam’s military campaigns.

articles.title: Kim Il Sung
articles.en: Kim Il Sung founded North Korea and ruled it from 1948 to 1994, establishing a hereditary authoritarian political system.

articles.title: Syngman Rhee
articles.en: Syngman Rhee was South Korea’s first president from 1948 to 1960, an anti-communist leader whose authoritarian rule sparked opposition.

articles.title: Park Chung-hee
articles.en: Park Chung-hee ruled South Korea from 1961 to 1979, overseeing rapid industrialization alongside political repression.

articles.title: Nelson Mandela
articles.en: Nelson Mandela was an anti-apartheid leader who spent 27 years imprisoned and became South Africa’s first Black president in 1994.

articles.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
articles.en: Martin Luther King Jr. was a US civil-rights leader known for nonviolent protest against racial segregation and discrimination.

articles.title: Malcolm X
articles.en: Malcolm X was a prominent African American activist whose views on Black liberation and human rights evolved during his life.

articles.title: John F. Kennedy
articles.en: John F. Kennedy was US president from 1961 until his assassination in 1963, serving during the Cuban Missile Crisis and early civil-rights struggles.

articles.title: Richard Nixon
articles.en: Richard Nixon was US president from 1969 to 1974, known for opening relations with China and resigning after the Watergate scandal.

articles.title: Ronald Reagan
articles.en: Ronald Reagan was US president from 1981 to 1989, associated with tax cuts, conservative politics and late Cold War diplomacy.

articles.title: Mikhail Gorbachev
articles.en: Mikhail Gorbachev was the final Soviet leader, associated with glasnost, perestroika and the peaceful end of much of the Cold War.

articles.title: Margaret Thatcher
articles.en: Margaret Thatcher was UK prime minister from 1979 to 1990, known for privatization, economic liberalization and confrontational political reforms.

articles.title: Queen Elizabeth II
articles.en: Elizabeth II was monarch of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms from 1952 until 2022, witnessing decades of constitutional and social change.

articles.title: Barack Obama
articles.en: Barack Obama served as US president from 2009 to 2017 and was the first African American to hold the office.

articles.title: Angela Merkel
articles.en: Angela Merkel was Germany’s chancellor from 2005 to 2021, playing a major role in European economic and political affairs.

articles.title: Xi Jinping
articles.en: Xi Jinping became China’s top Communist Party leader in 2012 and president in 2013, overseeing a more centralized political system and assertive foreign policy.

articles.title: Vladimir Putin
articles.en: Vladimir Putin has dominated Russian politics since 1999 as president or prime minister; his rule includes increasing authoritarianism and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Donald Trump
articles.en: Donald Trump served as US president from 2017 to 2021 and returned to office in January 2025. His political approach has reshaped American party politics and international relations.

articles.title: Joe Biden
articles.en: Joe Biden served as US president from 2021 to 2025, following a long career as senator and vice president.

articles.title: Albert Einstein
articles.en: Albert Einstein was a theoretical physicist whose relativity theories transformed modern physics and understanding of gravity, space and time.

articles.title: Marie Curie
articles.en: Marie Curie pioneered research on radioactivity and received Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry.

articles.title: Alan Turing
articles.en: Alan Turing was a mathematician and computer science pioneer who contributed to wartime codebreaking and the theoretical foundations of computing.

articles.title: Steve Jobs
articles.en: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple and helped popularize personal computers, digital music players and smartphones.

articles.title: Bill Gates
articles.en: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft and helped shape the personal computer software industry before focusing heavily on philanthropy.

articles.title: Tim Berners-Lee
articles.en: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN, proposing a system of linked hypertext documents.

articles.title: Malala Yousafzai
articles.en: Malala Yousafzai is a Pakistani education activist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate known for advocating girls’ access to schooling.

articles.title: Greta Thunberg
articles.en: Greta Thunberg is a Swedish climate activist who helped popularize youth-led school strikes for climate action.

articles.title: Beef bourguignon
articles.en: Beef slowly braised in red wine with carrots, onions, mushrooms and bacon; strongly associated with Burgundy and served in French bistros and home kitchens. Origin or strong culinary association: France.

articles.title: Bouillabaisse

articles.title: Ratatouille

articles.title: Cassoulet

articles.title: Quiche Lorraine
articles.en: A savory tart from Lorraine traditionally made with eggs, cream and bacon; commonly sold in French bakeries and cafés. Origin or strong culinary association: France.

articles.title: Croque monsieur

articles.title: Crêpe

articles.title: Soufflé

articles.title: Tarte tatin

articles.title: Escargots

articles.title: Steak frites

articles.title: Fondue

articles.title: Carbonara

articles.title: Cacio e pepe

articles.title: Lasagna

articles.title: Osso buco
articles.en: Cross-cut veal shanks braised with vegetables, wine and stock, especially associated with Milan and often served with risotto. Origin or strong culinary association: Italy.

articles.title: Tiramisu
articles.en: A layered Italian dessert of coffee-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone cream, dusted with cocoa. Origin or strong culinary association: Italy.

articles.title: Gnocchi
articles.en: Soft dumplings often made from potato and flour, served with sauces such as tomato, butter and sage or pesto. Origin or strong culinary association: Italy.

articles.title: Ravioli
articles.en: Stuffed pasta parcels containing fillings such as ricotta, spinach, meat or seafood, eaten throughout Italy with regional variations. Origin or strong culinary association: Italy.

articles.title: Pesto

articles.title: Focaccia

articles.title: Paella

articles.title: Gazpacho

articles.title: Tortilla española

articles.title: Patatas bravas

articles.title: Churros

articles.title: Bacalhau à brás
articles.en: Salt cod mixed with thin fried potatoes, onions and scrambled eggs, a traditional Portuguese dish. Origin or strong culinary association: Portugal.

articles.title: Pastel de nata
articles.en: A small flaky pastry tart filled with egg custard, associated with Lisbon and eaten across Portugal. Origin or strong culinary association: Portugal.

articles.title: Moussaka
articles.en: A baked casserole of eggplant, spiced minced meat and béchamel, especially associated with Greek home cooking. Origin or strong culinary association: Greece.

articles.title: Souvlaki
articles.en: Small skewers of grilled meat, commonly pork or chicken, served with pita and vegetables in Greece. Origin or strong culinary association: Greece.

articles.title: Spanakopita
articles.en: A savory Greek pastry of spinach and feta wrapped in crisp phyllo dough. Origin or strong culinary association: Greece.

articles.title: Baklava
articles.en: Layers of phyllo pastry, chopped nuts and syrup or honey; enjoyed across Turkey, Greece and the eastern Mediterranean. Origin or strong culinary association: Turkey and Eastern Mediterranean.

articles.title: Döner kebab
articles.en: Seasoned meat roasted on a vertical spit and shaved into bread or onto a plate; popular in Turkey and across Europe. Origin or strong culinary association: Turkey.

articles.title: Shakshuka
articles.en: Eggs poached in a spiced tomato-and-pepper sauce, commonly eaten for breakfast or brunch in North Africa and Israel. Origin or strong culinary association: North Africa and Middle East.

articles.title: Hummus
articles.en: A dip of cooked chickpeas, tahini, lemon and garlic, eaten throughout the Levant and beyond. Origin or strong culinary association: Levant.

articles.title: Falafel
articles.en: Fried balls or patties of ground chickpeas or fava beans with herbs and spices, served in pita or on platters. Origin or strong culinary association: Middle East.

articles.title: Tabbouleh
articles.en: A parsley-forward salad with tomatoes, bulgur, lemon and olive oil, strongly associated with Lebanon and Syria. Origin or strong culinary association: Levant.

articles.title: Biryani

articles.title: Butter chicken
articles.en: A North Indian dish of tandoori-style chicken in a creamy tomato-and-butter sauce, associated with Delhi. Origin or strong culinary association: India.

articles.title: Dosa
articles.en: A thin fermented rice-and-lentil crepe, often served with sambar and chutneys, popular across southern India. Origin or strong culinary association: South India.

articles.title: Idli
articles.en: Soft steamed cakes of fermented rice-and-lentil batter, commonly eaten at breakfast with chutney and sambar. Origin or strong culinary association: South India.

articles.title: Tandoori chicken
articles.en: Chicken marinated in yogurt and spices and cooked in a tandoor oven, popular in North Indian and Punjabi cuisine. Origin or strong culinary association: India.

articles.title: Dal
articles.en: A broad family of dishes made from cooked lentils, peas or beans, often tempered with spices and eaten with rice or bread. Origin or strong culinary association: South Asia.

articles.title: Nasi lemak
articles.en: Rice cooked in coconut milk and pandan, served with sambal, anchovies, peanuts, cucumber and egg, often with fried chicken. Origin or strong culinary association: Malaysia and Singapore.

articles.title: Hainanese chicken rice
articles.en: Poached or roasted chicken served with fragrant chicken-fat rice, chili sauce and ginger; an iconic Singapore hawker dish with Hainanese roots. Origin or strong culinary association: Singapore and Malaysia.

articles.title: Laksa
articles.en: A family of spicy noodle soups, including coconut-rich curry laksa and tangy fish-based asam laksa. Origin or strong culinary association: Singapore and Malaysia.

articles.title: Char kway teow
articles.en: Flat rice noodles stir-fried over high heat with egg, bean sprouts and sauces, often with seafood or Chinese sausage. Origin or strong culinary association: Singapore and Malaysia.

articles.title: Bak kut teh
articles.en: Pork rib soup with regional styles ranging from peppery Teochew broth to herbal Klang versions, typically served with rice and tea. Origin or strong culinary association: Singapore and Malaysia.

articles.title: Chili crab
articles.en: Crab cooked in a sweet, savory and mildly spicy tomato-chili sauce, often eaten with fried mantou buns. Origin or strong culinary association: Singapore.

articles.title: Fish head curry
articles.en: Fish head simmered in spiced curry with vegetables, a dish shaped by South Indian and local Singaporean influences. Origin or strong culinary association: Singapore and Malaysia.

articles.title: Roti prata
articles.en: A flaky griddled flatbread with South Asian roots, commonly eaten with curry or sugar. Origin or strong culinary association: Singapore and Malaysia.

articles.title: Satay
articles.en: Skewered grilled meat served with sauces, often peanut-based, popular in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. Origin or strong culinary association: Southeast Asia.

articles.title: Rendang
articles.en: Meat slowly cooked with coconut milk and aromatic spices until richly concentrated, associated with Minangkabau cuisine of West Sumatra. Origin or strong culinary association: Indonesia.

articles.title: Gado-gado
articles.en: A salad of cooked vegetables, tofu, tempeh and eggs dressed in peanut sauce, eaten throughout Indonesia. Origin or strong culinary association: Indonesia.

articles.title: Soto ayam
articles.en: A fragrant turmeric-colored chicken soup with noodles or rice, popular in Indonesia and neighboring countries. Origin or strong culinary association: Indonesia.

articles.title: Pho
articles.en: Vietnamese rice-noodle soup served in aromatic broth with beef or chicken and herbs, associated with northern Vietnam and enjoyed nationwide. Origin or strong culinary association: Vietnam.

articles.title: Banh mi
articles.en: A Vietnamese baguette sandwich with fillings such as pâté, pork, pickled vegetables and herbs, reflecting French and Vietnamese influences. Origin or strong culinary association: Vietnam.

articles.title: Bun cha
articles.en: Grilled pork served with rice vermicelli, herbs and dipping broth, especially associated with Hanoi. Origin or strong culinary association: Vietnam.

articles.title: Goi cuon
articles.en: Fresh Vietnamese rice-paper rolls with herbs, vermicelli and shrimp or pork, commonly served with dipping sauce. Origin or strong culinary association: Vietnam.

articles.title: Pad Thai
articles.en: Stir-fried rice noodles with tamarind, fish sauce, egg, tofu or shrimp and peanuts, a widely known Thai street-food dish. Origin or strong culinary association: Thailand.

articles.title: Tom yum
articles.en: A hot-and-sour Thai soup scented with lemongrass, galangal and lime leaves, often made with shrimp. Origin or strong culinary association: Thailand.

articles.title: Green curry
articles.en: A Thai coconut-milk curry flavored with green chilies and aromatic herbs, commonly served with rice. Origin or strong culinary association: Thailand.

articles.title: Som tam
articles.en: A spicy, sour green-papaya salad pounded with lime, chilies and fish sauce, associated with northeastern Thailand and Laos. Origin or strong culinary association: Thailand and Laos.

articles.title: Massaman curry
articles.en: A rich Thai curry with warming spices, coconut milk, potatoes and meat, reflecting Persian and South Asian influences. Origin or strong culinary association: Thailand.

articles.title: Sushi
articles.en: A Japanese dish centered on vinegared rice, served with seafood, vegetables or other toppings in styles such as nigiri and maki. Origin or strong culinary association: Japan.

articles.title: Sashimi
articles.en: Thin slices of raw seafood served without rice, commonly accompanied by soy sauce and wasabi in Japan. Origin or strong culinary association: Japan.

articles.title: Ramen
articles.en: Japanese wheat-noodle soup with broths such as shoyu, miso, shio or tonkotsu, served with meat and other toppings. Origin or strong culinary association: Japan.

articles.title: Udon
articles.en: Thick wheat noodles served hot in broth or chilled with dipping sauce, eaten across Japan. Origin or strong culinary association: Japan.

articles.title: Soba

articles.title: Tempura

articles.title: Takoyaki

articles.title: Tonkatsu
articles.en: Breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet served with shredded cabbage and thick sauce, a Japanese yoshoku staple. Origin or strong culinary association: Japan.

articles.title: Miso soup
articles.en: Soup made with fermented soybean paste dissolved in dashi, often containing tofu, seaweed or vegetables. Origin or strong culinary association: Japan.

articles.title: Kimchi

articles.title: Bibimbap

articles.title: Bulgogi

articles.title: Japchae

articles.title: Jajangmyeon

articles.title: Dim sum

articles.title: Feijoada
articles.en: A hearty black-bean stew with pork cuts, commonly served with rice, greens and orange slices in Brazil. Origin or strong culinary association: Brazil.

articles.title: Ceviche

articles.en: Corn tortillas filled with spit-roasted marinated pork, pineapple and garnishes, developed in Mexico with Lebanese influences. Origin or strong culinary association: Mexico.

articles.title: Mole poblano
articles.en: A complex Puebla-style sauce using dried chilies, spices and sometimes chocolate, often served with poultry. Origin or strong culinary association: Mexico.

articles.title: Poutine

articles.title: Atom
articles.en: An atom is the basic unit of a chemical element, made of a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons.

articles.title: Molecule
articles.en: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds, forming a distinct chemical entity.

articles.title: Electron
articles.en: An electron is a negatively charged elementary particle found around atomic nuclei and central to electricity and chemical bonding.

articles.title: Proton
articles.en: A proton is a positively charged particle in an atomic nucleus; its number defines the chemical element.

articles.title: Neutron
articles.en: A neutron is an electrically neutral particle found in most atomic nuclei and involved in nuclear stability.

articles.title: Periodic table
articles.en: The periodic table arranges chemical elements by atomic number and recurring properties, revealing patterns in chemical behavior.

articles.title: Hydrogen
articles.en: Hydrogen is the lightest chemical element, with atomic number 1; it is abundant in stars and used in industrial chemistry.

articles.title: Oxygen
articles.en: Oxygen is a chemical element essential to most animal respiration and a major component of water and Earth's atmosphere.

articles.title: Carbon
articles.en: Carbon is an element able to form diverse chemical bonds and is central to organic chemistry and life.

articles.title: Nitrogen
articles.en: Nitrogen is a chemical element making up most of Earth's atmosphere and used in fertilizers and many biological molecules.

articles.title: Iron
articles.en: Iron is a metallic element widely used in steel production and essential to hemoglobin in human blood.

articles.title: Gold
articles.en: Gold is a relatively unreactive precious metal used in jewelry, electronics and monetary reserves.

articles.title: Silver
articles.en: Silver is a conductive precious metal used in jewelry, electronics and industrial applications.

articles.title: Copper
articles.en: Copper is a conductive metal used in electrical wiring, plumbing and alloys such as bronze.

articles.title: Silicon
articles.en: Silicon is a semiconductor element used in computer chips and solar cells, and a major constituent of many minerals.

articles.title: Lithium
articles.en: Lithium is a lightweight alkali metal used in rechargeable batteries and other industrial applications.

articles.title: Sodium
articles.en: Sodium is a highly reactive alkali metal; its compounds, including sodium chloride, are important in biology and industry.

articles.title: Chlorine
articles.en: Chlorine is a reactive halogen used in water treatment and chemical production, often in compounds such as chloride salts.

articles.title: Calcium
articles.en: Calcium is a chemical element important for bones, teeth, muscle function and numerous minerals.

articles.title: Photosynthesis
articles.en: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to make organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water.

articles.title: Cellular respiration
articles.en: Cellular respiration converts energy in food molecules into ATP, often using oxygen in eukaryotic cells.

articles.title: RNA
articles.en: RNA is a nucleic acid involved in gene expression and protein production; some viruses use RNA as genetic material.

articles.title: Gene
articles.en: A gene is a DNA sequence that contributes to a functional product, such as an RNA or protein.

articles.title: Chromosome
articles.en: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule packaged with proteins that carries genetic information.

articles.title: Genome
articles.en: A genome is an organism's complete set of genetic material.

articles.title: Mutation
articles.en: A mutation is a change in genetic sequence that may have neutral, harmful or beneficial effects.

articles.title: Natural selection
articles.en: Natural selection occurs when heritable traits influence survival or reproduction, changing their frequency over generations.

articles.title: Ecosystem
articles.en: An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with one another and their physical environment.

articles.title: Food chain
articles.en: A food chain traces energy and nutrient transfer between organisms through feeding relationships.

articles.title: Climate
articles.en: Climate is the long-term pattern of weather conditions in a region, commonly assessed over decades.

articles.title: Weather
articles.en: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions including temperature, rain, wind and humidity.

articles.title: Greenhouse effect
articles.en: The greenhouse effect is warming caused by atmospheric gases absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation; human emissions strengthen it.

articles.title: Carbon dioxide
articles.en: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas produced by respiration, combustion and other processes; it is used by plants in photosynthesis.

articles.title: Methane
articles.en: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas released from natural and human sources, including wetlands, livestock and fossil fuel operations.

articles.title: Ocean currents
articles.en: Ocean currents are large-scale movements of seawater driven by wind, density differences and Earth's rotation.

articles.title: Plate tectonics
articles.en: Plate tectonics explains the movement of Earth's lithospheric plates and processes such as earthquakes, volcanism and mountain building.

articles.title: Volcano
articles.en: A volcano is an opening where molten rock, gases and ash reach Earth's surface.

articles.title: Tropical cyclone
articles.en: A tropical cyclone is a rotating storm system forming over warm tropical oceans, called a hurricane or typhoon in some regions.

articles.title: Monsoon
articles.en: A monsoon is a seasonal shift in prevailing winds, often bringing pronounced wet and dry periods.

articles.title: El Niño
articles.en: El Niño is a recurring warming of central and eastern tropical Pacific waters that influences weather patterns worldwide.

articles.title: La Niña
articles.en: La Niña is a recurring cooling of central and eastern tropical Pacific waters that influences global climate patterns.

articles.title: Velocity
articles.en: Velocity is the rate of change of position with direction, measured as displacement per unit time.

articles.title: Acceleration
articles.en: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes over time.

articles.title: Momentum
articles.en: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity, conserved in isolated systems.

articles.title: Kinetic energy
articles.en: Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due to motion.

articles.title: Potential energy
articles.en: Potential energy is stored energy associated with position or configuration, such as gravitational or elastic energy.

articles.title: Thermodynamics
articles.en: Thermodynamics studies heat, work, energy and their transformations in physical systems.

articles.title: Entropy
articles.en: Entropy measures aspects of energy dispersal or the number of microscopic configurations compatible with a system's state.

articles.title: Electromagnetism
articles.en: Electromagnetism describes interactions involving electric charges, currents and magnetic fields.

articles.title: Electric current
articles.en: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.

articles.title: Voltage
articles.en: Voltage is electric potential difference between two points, measured in volts.

articles.title: Resistance
articles.en: Electrical resistance describes opposition to current flow, measured in ohms.

articles.title: Semiconductor
articles.en: A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled, enabling transistors and integrated circuits.

articles.title: Transistor
articles.en: A transistor is a semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electrical signals, fundamental to modern electronics.

articles.title: Microprocessor
articles.en: A microprocessor is a programmable integrated circuit that executes instructions and performs computation.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence
articles.en: Artificial intelligence is a field of computing focused on systems performing tasks associated with perception, reasoning, prediction or generation.

articles.title: Neural network
articles.en: An artificial neural network is a computational model of connected units that learns patterns by adjusting parameters.

articles.title: Large language model
articles.en: A large language model is a neural network trained on text and other data to predict and generate language.

articles.title: Internet
articles.en: The internet is a global network of interconnected computer networks communicating through standardized protocols.

articles.title: World Wide Web
articles.en: The World Wide Web is a system of linked documents and resources accessed over the internet using web technologies.

articles.title: HTTP
articles.en: HTTP is an application protocol for exchanging requests and responses between web clients and servers.

articles.title: Encryption
articles.en: Encryption transforms readable data into encoded form that can be reversed with an appropriate key.

articles.title: Cryptography
articles.en: Cryptography studies techniques for secure communication, authentication and data integrity.

articles.title: Blockchain
articles.en: A blockchain is a distributed record structure linking blocks of data cryptographically, used in some digital asset systems.

articles.title: Database
articles.en: A database is an organized collection of information designed for storage, retrieval and updating.

articles.title: Algorithm
articles.en: An algorithm is a defined sequence of steps for solving a problem or performing a computation.

articles.title: Solar system
articles.en: The solar system consists of the Sun and objects gravitationally bound to it, including eight planets and smaller bodies.

articles.title: Galaxy
articles.en: A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter.

articles.title: Black hole
articles.en: A black hole is a region of spacetime from which light cannot escape beyond the event horizon.

articles.title: Neutron star
articles.en: A neutron star is an extremely dense remnant formed after certain massive stars undergo supernova explosions.

articles.title: Supernova
articles.en: A supernova is a powerful stellar explosion that can occur in different ways, including massive star collapse.

articles.title: Big Bang
articles.en: The Big Bang model describes the universe's expansion from an early hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago.

articles.title: Light-year
articles.en: A light-year is a unit of distance equal to how far light travels in a vacuum in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers.

articles.title: Relativity
articles.en: Relativity is Einstein's framework describing spacetime, motion and gravitation through special and general relativity.

articles.title: Quantum mechanics
articles.en: Quantum mechanics describes physical behavior at atomic and subatomic scales using probabilistic mathematical models.

articles.title: Nuclear fission
articles.en: Nuclear fission splits a heavy atomic nucleus into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and often neutrons.

articles.title: Nuclear fusion
articles.en: Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei into heavier nuclei, releasing energy under suitable conditions, as in stars.

articles.title: Vaccination
articles.en: Vaccination trains the immune system to recognize specific pathogens or their components, reducing risk of certain infections.

articles.title: Immune system
articles.en: The immune system is a network of cells, tissues and molecules that protects the body from infections and other threats.

articles.title: Virus
articles.en: A virus is an infectious agent that reproduces using the machinery of host cells.

articles.title: Bacterium
articles.en: A bacterium is a single-celled microorganism; many are harmless or beneficial, while some cause disease.

articles.title: Antibiotic
articles.en: An antibiotic is a medicine used against bacterial infections; antibiotics do not treat viral infections.

articles.title: Antibiotic resistance
articles.en: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve or acquire mechanisms that reduce the effectiveness of antibiotics.

articles.title: Diabetes
articles.en: Diabetes is a group of conditions involving persistently high blood glucose due to impaired insulin production or action.

articles.title: Hypertension
articles.en: Hypertension is persistently elevated blood pressure and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

articles.title: Protein
articles.en: Proteins are molecules built from amino acids and serve structural, enzymatic, signaling and other biological roles.

articles.title: Carbohydrate
articles.en: Carbohydrates are sugars, starches and fibers that provide energy and perform other biological functions.

articles.title: Fat
articles.en: Dietary fats are nutrients important for energy storage, cell membranes and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

articles.title: Vitamin
articles.en: Vitamins are organic micronutrients needed in small amounts for normal physiological function.

articles.title: Mineral nutrient
articles.en: Mineral nutrients are inorganic elements needed for bodily functions, such as iron, calcium and potassium.
